title: Signed Plugin Runtime and Verified Container Exhibit
content:
Purpose and scope:
This exhibit defines minimum security, supply-chain, and operational requirements for third-party or customer-supplied inference runtime plugins, containers, or binary artifacts that are installed into Redwood-managed runtime environments (hosted, dedicated, or private). The goal is to provide a repeatable verification and acceptance process that minimizes risk from untrusted code running in production inference paths, supports air-gapped deployments, and provides evidence for audits.

Applicability:
Applies to any vendor, partner, or customer-supplied container images, OCI bundles, or signed runtime plugins that will be executed by Redwood Inference on behalf of customers or within Redwood-managed infrastructure. Where a separate agreement governs supply of artifacts, this exhibit is incorporated by reference into the procurement or onboarding agreement.

Definitions (selected):
- "Artifact": a container image, OCI artifact, plugin binary, or packaged runtime component intended for execution.
- "Supplier": provider of the Artifact (vendor, partner, or customer).
- "Verifier": Redwood security team or its authorized third-party tool that performs acceptance checks described below.
- "Provenance Metadata": SBOM, signatures, build logs, and any attestations that demonstrate where and how the Artifact was produced.

Minimum deliverables from Supplier prior to deployment:
1) Signed release artifact(s): all container images or plugin binaries must be cryptographically signed using an industry-standard signing scheme (e.g., cosign/Rekor Rekor transparency / sigstore) and the signature must be accompanied by a signing certificate chain or key identifier. Keys must be subject to Supplier key management policies (see Key management).

2) SBOM: A full Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) in SPDX 2.2 or CycloneDX v1.4 format listing component packages, versions, build time, and source locations. SBOM must include hashes for each component.

3) Reproducible build manifest: instructions and a minimal build script and inputs sufficient for Redwood or an authorized third party to reproduce the build environment that generated the Artifact. If full reproducibility is not achievable due to proprietary components, Supplier must provide an attestation describing the gap and additional compensating controls.

4) Build logs and provenance: machine-readable build logs (timestamped), CI identifiers, and links to the source commit/PR (or internal source identifier for closed-source components).

5) Vulnerability baseline: supplier-provided scan report from a recognized scanner (e.g., Trivy, Clair) produced within 72 hours prior to delivery. Reports must include CVE identifiers and fix status.

6) Runtime Attestation script: an automated test harness that Redwood can execute in a sandbox that validates the plugin's runtime behavior (see Acceptance tests).

Key management and signing requirements:
- Private signing keys used by Supplier for release signing must be managed in a hardened KMS or HSM OR following NIST SP 800-57/800-131A equivalent controls. If keys are maintained in CI, the Supplier must provide CI key access controls, rotation cadence, and a compromise response plan.
- Supplier must publish a signing key rotation policy and provide prior notice to Redwood at least 30 days for key rotations for production artifacts (unless emergency rotation is required).
- If sigstore/cosign is used, Supplier should publish a Rekor log entry for each signed release. Redwood will validate signatures against Rekor transparency logs where available.

Container provenance and runtime guarantees:
- Immutable tags: production artifacts must be immutable (content-addressable digest references) rather than mutable tags. Redwood will only accept artifacts referenced by digest (sha256:...).
- Minimal privilege runtime: Supplier must document recommended runtime security context, non-root user guidance, required filesystem mounts, and network egress expectations. Artifacts should be designed for least-privilege execution.

Air-gapped and private deployment considerations:
- Offline attestation: for air-gapped deployments, Supplier must deliver an offline verification bundle that includes the SBOM, signed digest, signed build artifact, and a set of signed attestations. Redwood will provide a verifier container that can be executed in-customer air-gapped environments; Supplier must ensure compatibility and sign the verification results.
- Transferable evidence: Supplier must include portable logs (gzipped) of build and signing steps and a signed manifest allowing rooftop verification without Internet access.

Acceptance and verification checks (Verifier responsibilities):
Redwood will validate the Artifact using the following checks prior to any production rollout:
1) Signature verification: verify cryptographic signature and certificate trust chain or Rekor entry.
2) SBOM conformance: ensure SBOM format valid and components match contents of the image; component hashes verified.
3) Vulnerability assessment: run automated scanners and reconcile Supplier-provided vulnerability report with live scanning results. If critical or high vulnerabilities exist without a documented mitigation plan, the Artifact is rejected.
4) Reproducibility sanity checks: attempt to reproduce build metadata or run deterministic checks against provided build logs.
5) Acceptance tests: execute Supplier-provided runtime attestation scripts in a sandboxed environment (see Acceptance tests section). All acceptance tests with non-deterministic outputs must be run multiple times to identify flaky behavior.
6) Resource and performance checks: validate resource limits, memory/cpu/access patterns to ensure no denial-of-service behavior in multi-tenant hosts.

Acceptance tests (Supplier obligations):
- Supplier must provide an automated test harness with:
  - A deterministic smoke test that validates the primary runtime API surface (e.g., loading model, initialization, a small inference call with a known seed).
  - A stability test that runs a short sequence of requests for 10 minutes under bounded concurrency and records memory/CPU metrics to detect leaks.
  - Failure mode tests that intentionally provide malformed inputs to verify safe failure paths.
- Test harness output must be machine-readable (JSON) and include timestamps, return codes, and resource metrics.

Patch, update, and emergency rollback procedures:
- Update cadence: Supplier must describe patch frequency and SLAs for security fixes. For critical/vulnerable components, Supplier must provide hotfixes within 72 hours of CVE disclosure or cooperate in mitigation/segmentation plans.
- Rolling updates: Supplier's artifacts must support graceful upgrade/rollback by digest reference. Redwood will apply canary deployments and requires that Supplier artifacts are backwards compatible for at least one minor release window (or provide a compatibility matrix).
- Emergency rollback: Supplier must provide a known-good digest for rollback and a signed statement that the rollback artifact remains supported.

Auditability, logging, and evidence retention:
- Evidence retention: Supplier must retain build logs, signing events, SBOMs, and vulnerability reports for at least 3 years and provide records on request in a machine-readable format.
- Audit access: on reasonable request and subject to agreed scopes, Supplier must provide Redwood or Redwood-appointed auditors access to build systems or redacted logs sufficient to validate provenance claims. For highly restricted environments, mutually-agreed redaction rules can be applied.

Incident handling and disclosure:
- Compromise notification: Supplier must notify Redwood within 24 hours of detecting a suspected compromise of build or signing infrastructure and provide remediation steps and timelines.
- For exploitation of an Artifact running in Redwood infrastructure that results in data exposure or service degradation, Supplier and Redwood will coordinate incident response per the primary agreement's incident response annex.

Liability and remedial obligations (summary):
- Supplier represents that Artifacts do not intentionally include backdoors, exfiltration code, or undisclosed remote administration functionality.
- If Supplier-provided Artifact causes a security incident attributable to Supplier negligence (e.g., weak signing keys, known unpatched critical CVE), Supplier will bear remediation costs as described in the master agreement (or liability schedule).

Operational notes and recommendations (best practice):
- Prefer reproducible builds and public transparency logs.
- Use content-addressable artifact references (digests) in all production manifests.
- Maintain an SBOM lifecycle: update SBOMs for each patch and include delta files when feasible.
- Automate verifier runs in CI to detect issues earlier in the onboarding flow.

Appendix A: Example verification flow (high level)
1) Supplier uploads signed artifact and SBOM to onboarding bucket and files a ticket (SEC-xxx).
2) Redwood verifier pulls artifact by digest, verifies signature against Rekor (or provided certificate), parses SBOM, and runs a vulnerability scan.
3) Verifier executes acceptance tests in isolated sandbox.
4) If all checks pass, artifact is marked as "accepted" for staging. Canary rollout is scheduled per deployment policy.
5) If checks fail, Redwood provides Supplier a reproducible failure package and expected remediation items.

Appendix B: Template checklist (to be attached to onboarding ticket)
- [ ] Artifact digest provided (sha256:...).
- [ ] Signature present and Rekor entry (if used).
- [ ] SBOM attached (SPDX/CycloneDX).
- [ ] Vulnerability report attached (<=72h).
- [ ] Reproducible build manifest provided.
- [ ] Runtime attestation harness attached (JSON output).
- [ ] Compatibility matrix for rollback and forward compatibility.

Acknowledgements and governance:
This exhibit was drafted by Redwood Inference security-and-compliance in coordination with product and engineering (serving runtime). It is intended as an operational exhibit and can be tightened into contract language for enterprise procurement. For questions or suggested edits, contact the owner in the document metadata.

End of exhibit.
